I can’t help write explicit sexual content involving coercive workplace abuse, forced penetration/restraints, or harm/disappearance presented erotically.

If you want, I can help turn the premise into a **dark, non-graphic dystopian office horror/satire** with BDSM-inspired aesthetics, power imbalance, and macabre ritual elements—without explicit sexual acts. For example:

---

In the city’s lower corporate districts, the clerks of Department Nine wore uniforms designed less for comfort than for symbolism. Their glossy black latex jackets mimicked ordinary office blazers, complete with sharp lapels and immaculate cuffs, but every seam was too tight, every collar too high, every movement accompanied by a soft, rubbery creak. Their identification badges were not clipped to pockets—there were no pockets—but fixed to metal rings on the uniform itself, displaying employee number, division, productivity grade, and disciplinary record.

Mara worked at a workstation known as a “compliance desk.” It resembled a normal cubicle from a distance: monitor, keyboard, lamp, stack of forms. Up close, nothing was quite right. The chair forced a rigid posture. The desk locked around the waist once the employee signed in. The keyboard only responded when both wrists were secured to the polished steel rests. The screen watched back.

Her work was not accounting, not correspondence, not scheduling—at least not in the normal sense. She processed confession summaries, corrected loyalty statements, indexed disciplinary footage, and updated the absence ledger whenever an employee failed to return from “review.” Each completed file earned her a fraction of comfort: a looser collar setting, a sip of water, five minutes under the warm air vent. Each mistake tightened some part of the station.

The office looked almost elegant. Rows of shining workers sat beneath cold fluorescent lights, their uniforms reflecting the glow like wet ink. Supervisors moved between them in matte grey coats, silent except for the click of their boots and the soft chime of their authority keys. No one gossiped. No one laughed. The only permitted conversation was procedural.

At night, the clerks were stored in the dormitory archive.

It was called a dormitory because the company manual insisted on the word, but it looked more like a wardrobe built for bodies. Each employee was sealed into a numbered rest-sleeve, suspended vertically in a narrow compartment. The material held them upright and motionless, preserving posture, conserving space, preventing “unauthorized fatigue behaviors.” A breathing valve, a nutrient line, a biometric reader, and the faint hum of circulating air were the only signs that the figures inside were sleeping rather than filed away.

For Mara, morning was a relief.

When the compartment opened and the supervisor’s gloved hand released the seals, the workday felt almost merciful by comparison. At least at the desk she could see. At least she could hear other keys tapping. At least her productivity bar could move upward.

Every Friday, the office held the Audit.

No one knew when it would happen, only that the lights would dim and the ceiling speakers would play the old company anthem in a warped, music-box tone. Then the supervisor would walk the aisle with a silver tablet, stopping before one workstation or one dormitory sleeve. The chosen employee’s records vanished from the system before the person did.

Officially, they were “promoted beyond visibility.”

Unofficially, the remaining clerks noticed things.

A vacant desk cleaned too quickly. A badge number reassigned by Monday. A faint smell of disinfectant near the freight elevator. Once, Mara found a single black glove caught beneath a filing cabinet, its fingertips stiff with something that had dried dark.

No one asked questions. Questions were a category of inefficiency.

Instead, Mara typed faster.

Her responsibilities expanded after her third month. She became an absence reconciler, which meant she altered schedules to account for employees who had never existed. She erased lunch allocations, reassigned workloads, updated personnel histories, and sent cheerful internal memos congratulating departments on improved space utilization. Her language had to be bright, neutral, corporate.

“Team capacity has been optimized.”

“Legacy roles have transitioned.”

“Operational silence has improved by twelve percent.”

By then, Mara understood the real purpose of Department Nine. It did not produce reports; it produced obedience. It turned fear into forms, exhaustion into metrics, disappearance into policy.

And every morning, when the rest-sleeve opened and the office lights burned white across the polished floor, Mara stepped back into her station with trembling gratitude—because in that place, work was the closest thing to freedom anyone was allowed to want.

---
